title: Who Am I?
theme: Identity and belonging: fitting in, standing apart
objectives: I can use identity, ancestry, and persona to talk about who people are and how they present themselves.
I can tell assimilate, conform, and integrate apart by what a person or group gives up and what each one gains.
I can explain how a group can alienate or marginalize people, and how solidarity works against that.
I can use the parts con-, intro-, -ate, and -ize to understand and build words about belonging.
rationale: Identity is a central theme in grade 8 literature and social studies, and these ten words capture the pull between belonging and difference. They fall into three groups: what makes a person who they are (identity, ancestry, persona, introspective), how people fit into groups (assimilate, conform, integrate), and what happens when belonging fails or succeeds (alienate, marginalize, solidarity). Assimilate, conform, and integrate are taught together on purpose because each describes a different relationship between a person and a group, and students will need the distinctions to read novels, memoirs, and history texts about immigration and community. The passage uses a fictional new student so that students can name what they see without the words being tied to any real group. The unit builds on testimony, context, conscience, and perception from earlier units, because identity is told through personal accounts that students must read in context.

words.def: The set of qualities, beliefs, and connections that make a person or group who they are.
words.ex: Language, family, and the places we call home all help shape a person's identity.
words.ex2: Her identity as a musician grew stronger every time she played for an audience.
words.nonExample: A name tag shows what someone is called, but it does not describe their whole identity.

apps.academic: In a memoir, the writer's identity often comes from family stories, language, and the places the writer has lived.
apps.spoken: My identity isn't just one thing; it's a lot of things.
apps.writing: Use identity for the qualities and connections that make someone who they are, and give an example of one.

cloze.s: Moving to a new country made Amina think carefully about which parts of her ___ she wanted to keep.

cloze2.s: A school's mascot, colors, and songs give students a shared ___ that makes them feel part of a group.

misuse.s: A person's identity can never include any beliefs, family, or culture.
misuse.why: Identity is made up of beliefs, family, and culture, among other things.

words.frame: One part of my identity is ___ because ___.

words.def: To become part of a larger group or culture by taking on its customs, language, or habits.
words.ex: Many families work to assimilate into a new community while still keeping the traditions they brought with them.
words.ex2: The new student tried to assimilate by dressing like her classmates and joining their club.
words.nonExample: Keeping your own customs and refusing any change is not assimilating.

apps.academic: Historians debate how much newcomers should assimilate and how much a community should adapt to them.
apps.spoken: She's trying to assimilate, but she misses her old school's traditions.
apps.writing: Use assimilate for taking on a group's ways, and ask what the person keeps and what they give up.

cloze.s: To ___ into the new school, Noor copied how her classmates talked and what they wore.

cloze2.s: Some immigrants choose to ___ quickly, while others hold tightly to the language and customs of their old home.

misuse.s: She assimilated by refusing to speak, dress, or act like anyone in the new group.
misuse.why: To assimilate is to take on a group's ways; refusing them is the opposite.

visual.alt: A puzzle piece fitting into a neighborhood scene.

words.frame: To assimilate, a newcomer might ___ but could lose ___.

words.def: The family line you come from, including your parents, grandparents, and earlier relatives.
words.ex: Her ancestry includes farmers, sailors, and a great-grandmother who taught school.
words.ex2: A class project asked students to trace their ancestry using family stories and old photographs.
words.nonExample: Your favorite hobby is part of who you are, but it is not part of your ancestry.

apps.academic: Writers sometimes explore their ancestry to understand why their family speaks, cooks, or celebrates as it does.
apps.spoken: My ancestry is a mix of three countries.
apps.writing: Use ancestry for the line of family before you, and name one detail that shows it.

cloze.s: Using old letters, Marco traced his ___ back four generations to a village in the mountains.

cloze2.s: On the family tree, the branches show how one person's ___ connects to many relatives.

misuse.s: Her ancestry is the list of friends she met last year.
misuse.why: Ancestry is the family line before you, not recent friends.

visual.alt: A family tree with portraits on its branches.

words.frame: My ancestry includes ___, which is why ___.

words.def: To follow the rules, customs, or behavior that a group expects.
words.ex: Students often conform to the clothing styles of their friends without ever discussing it.
words.ex2: The factory had to conform to new safety rules before it could reopen.
words.nonExample: Wearing a bright costume to school when no one else does is not conforming.

apps.academic: A character who refuses to conform often creates the conflict in a story about belonging.
apps.spoken: I don't want to conform just to be liked.
apps.writing: Use conform for following expected behavior, and say whether the pressure comes from people or from rules.

cloze.s: Even though she liked the old song, she tried to ___ and pretend to like what her friends liked.

cloze2.s: All new buildings in the town must ___ to the fire code.

misuse.s: He conformed by deliberately doing the opposite of whatever his group did.
misuse.why: To conform is to follow what a group expects, not to do the opposite.

visual.alt: Sheep following one another in a line.

words.def: To make someone feel like an outsider or unwelcome, or to turn someone against you.
words.ex: The coach's constant sarcasm began to alienate the youngest players on the team.
words.ex2: A group that mocks newcomers will alienate the very people it hopes to attract.
words.nonExample: Inviting a new classmate to join your table does not alienate her.

apps.academic: Authors show alienation by placing a character at the edge of a group, watching but not joining.
apps.spoken: Don't alienate your teammates by blaming them.
apps.writing: Use alienate for actions that push people away, and name who is alienated and by what.

cloze.s: Posting inside jokes that only some classmates understand can ___ the others.

cloze2.s: The manager's habit of ignoring suggestions began to ___ the workers who had once been loyal.

misuse.s: The club alienated new members by inviting them in, explaining the rules, and saving them a seat.
misuse.why: To alienate is to push people away; inviting and helping them does the opposite.

visual.alt: A person standing alone outside a closed door.

words.def: Unity and support among people who share a goal, a condition, or a struggle.
words.ex: Students wore blue on Friday to show solidarity with a classmate who was recovering in the hospital.
words.ex2: The workers' solidarity helped them win a safer schedule, because no one broke ranks.
words.nonExample: Walking away from a group when things get hard is not solidarity.

apps.academic: Acts of solidarity, such as a shared silence or a joint letter, show that a group stands behind one of its members.
apps.spoken: We stayed to show solidarity with the team.
apps.writing: Use solidarity for support among people who share a cause, and name an action that shows it.

cloze.s: The whole team stayed after the game in ___ with the injured player, refusing to celebrate until she was safe.

cloze2.s: Neighbors showed ___ by bringing meals, tools, and rides to the family whose house had burned.

misuse.s: Solidarity means each person acts alone and refuses to help anyone else.
misuse.why: Solidarity is standing together, not acting alone.

visual.alt: Clasped hands beside a raised fist.

words.def: To bring different groups or parts together so that they work or live as one whole.
words.ex: The school worked to integrate its clubs so that students from different grades could join the same activities.
words.ex2: New software can integrate the library's records with the classroom roster.
words.nonExample: Keeping two groups in separate buildings does not integrate them.

apps.academic: Integrate can describe a community making room for newcomers as full members, not asking them to disappear.
apps.spoken: We need to integrate the new players into the team.
apps.writing: Use integrate for joining groups or parts into a working whole, and name what is joined.

cloze.s: The new community center was designed to ___ neighbors of every age, so children and elders shared one lively space.

cloze2.s: A good teacher finds ways to ___ new students into the class routine during the first week.

misuse.s: The principal integrated the groups by building a wall to keep them apart.
misuse.why: To integrate is to bring together; a wall keeps groups apart.

visual.alt: A chain linking two groups of people.

words.frame: To integrate ___ and ___, a group could ___.

words.def: To treat a person or group as unimportant, pushing them to the edges of a society or a conversation.
words.ex: When the planning committee never asked the youngest residents for ideas, it marginalized them.
words.ex2: A history book that leaves out entire communities can marginalize them, even when no one intends it.
words.nonExample: Asking every member for ideas does not marginalize anyone.

apps.academic: Sociologists ask which groups are marginalized in a decision and what it would take to include them.
apps.spoken: I felt marginalized because no one asked what I thought.
apps.writing: Use marginalize for pushing a group out of decisions or attention, and name who is affected and how.

cloze.s: Scheduling every event in the old building, which has no ramp, would ___ students who use wheelchairs.

cloze2.s: Meetings held only in the afternoon can ___ parents who work until evening.

misuse.s: The club marginalized the new members by giving them the lead roles and asking for their ideas first.
misuse.why: To marginalize is to push people aside; giving leadership and asking for ideas includes them.

visual.alt: A person standing at the edge of a circle of people.

words.frame: A group marginalizes people when it ___.

words.def: The public character or image a person shows to others, which may differ from who they are in private.
words.ex: On stage the singer took on a bold, fiery persona that was nothing like her quiet, shy self.
words.ex2: Many people build an online persona that shows only the best parts of their lives.
words.nonExample: Your private thoughts, which no one sees, are not part of your persona.

apps.academic: A narrator's persona can differ from the author's own voice, so readers should ask who is speaking.
apps.spoken: His online persona is totally different from how he is in person.
apps.writing: Use persona for the image someone presents, and compare it with the person underneath.

cloze.s: At work he kept a serious ___, but at home he joked constantly.

cloze2.s: The author wrote under a mysterious ___ so that readers would not know her real name.

misuse.s: A persona is the unchanging private self that no one ever sees.
misuse.why: A persona is the public image a person shows, not the private self.

visual.alt: A theater mask in front of a smiling face.

words.frame: The persona of ___ is ___ but the person is ___.

words.def: Inclined to look inward and examine your own thoughts and feelings.
words.ex: After the argument, Dev grew introspective and spent the evening thinking about what he had said.
words.ex2: The poem's introspective tone invites readers to examine their own doubts and hopes.
words.nonExample: Joking loudly with friends at a party is not an introspective moment.

apps.academic: An introspective narrator tells the story by examining her own motives and memories.
apps.spoken: I get introspective when I'm alone at night.
apps.writing: Use introspective for someone who examines their own thoughts, often in writing or quiet thinking.

cloze.s: The ___ student kept a journal in which she questioned why she had reacted so strongly to the news.

cloze2.s: A quiet walk along the river made him ___, and he began to ask what he truly wanted from the year ahead.

misuse.s: She was introspective, so she never once thought about her own feelings or motives.
misuse.why: Introspective means examining your own thoughts and feelings, not ignoring them.

visual.alt: A mirror reflecting a thinking person.

passage.title: Noor's Recipe Cards
paras: When Noor's family moved to Cedar Hills in October, she carried a backpack, a box of her grandmother's recipe cards, and a question she had not said aloud: who would she be here? At her old school, everyone knew her identity. She was the girl who loved chess and spoke two languages at home. At Cedar Hills, nobody knew either fact.

Her cousin Layla had given advice. "Just assimilate," she said. "Do what they do, and nobody will notice you." So at lunch Noor laughed at jokes she did not find funny, left her chess book at home, and spoke only English, even to the cafeteria worker who greeted her in her home language. She tried to conform in every small way she could.

By November, she barely recognized the persona she had built: cheerful, easygoing, and invisible. Her grandmother noticed it right away on a video call. "Tell me about your ancestry," she said suddenly. "Do you remember whose recipes those are?" Noor looked at the cards on her desk, written in three generations of handwriting.

The next week she stayed for chess club and found Mr. Bell building a team of students who felt alienated by the school's sports culture. "We are not the usual crowd," said a boy named Eli, "but we show up for each other." Noor had not felt that kind of solidarity in weeks. Mr. Bell added that a small club should never be marginalized just because it was small, so he had asked the principal for a page in the yearbook.

At the winter festival, the school tried to integrate every club into one big fair. Noor's table held chess boards beside a plate of her grandmother's cookies. That night, feeling introspective, she wrote in her journal: "A place can make room for me without changing me."

qs.q: In paragraph 2, Layla's advice to "assimilate" most nearly means to
choices: move to a different school
blend into the group by taking on its ways
keep to yourself and avoid everyone
refuse to follow any group's rules
qs.why: Layla explains it as doing what the others do so that no one notices Noor, which means blending in.

qs.q: Why does Noor's grandmother ask her to "tell me about your ancestry"?
choices: She wants to learn about Noor's new teachers.
She notices that Noor has hidden parts of her identity and wants to remind her where she comes from.
She is planning a family reunion.
She wants Noor to stop cooking.
qs.why: The grandmother notices the change on the video call and points to the recipe cards written by three generations, which tie Noor to her family history.

qs.q: Which detail best shows solidarity among the chess club members?
choices: The club needed a page in the yearbook.
Mr. Bell was the advisor.
Eli says the members show up for each other.
Noor's table was beside a plate of cookies.
qs.why: Eli's remark shows the members support one another, and the passage names the feeling solidarity.

qs.q: What does Noor mean when she writes, "A place can make room for me without changing me"?
choices: She wants to leave Cedar Hills.
She thinks other students should change to match her.
She believes she can belong without giving up who she is.
She no longer wants to take part in chess club.
qs.why: After trying to conform and becoming invisible, Noor finds a club and a table where she can be herself, so she believes she can belong without changing.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: New students should always avoid joining clubs.
A person can belong to a community without hiding the parts of their identity that matter to them.
Family advice is usually wrong.
Sports are more important than chess in schools.
qs.why: Noor tries to hide her identity to fit in, then discovers a group where she can be herself and still belong.

constructed.prompt: A new student joins a class. One classmate tells her to dress and act like everyone else, another says she must follow the class rules, and a third invites her to share her traditions with the whole class. Use assimilate, conform, and integrate to match each classmate's advice.

explains the difference among the three

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for talking about identity and belonging, read a short narrative about a new student deciding how much to change, practice the prefixes con- and intro- and the suffixes -ate and -ize, and write about fitting in. The unit's habit is to ask what a person keeps, what a group asks them to give up, and what would make the group more welcoming.

notes.va.identity.n: Identity is made of many parts, such as family, language, interests, and beliefs. Avoid asking students to disclose personal details; invite fictional or chosen examples. Show that identity can have more than one part by building a web with a character.
notes.va.assimilate.v: Assimilate means taking on a group's customs. Keep it neutral: it can be a choice or a pressure. Ask 'what does the person keep, and what do they give up?' Compare with integrate, where the group also changes.
notes.va.ancestry.n: Ancestry is the family line before you. Some students may not know their family histories, and some may have complicated ones; offer an alternative such as 'a character's ancestry' or 'a family you invent'. Link to the family on the word card.
notes.va.conform.v: Conform means following expected behavior. It is neutral: conforming to a safety rule is good; conforming to harmful pressure is not. Model con- + form ('shape together'). Ask students to name two situations that call for conformity and two that do not.
notes.va.alienate.v: Alienate is to push someone away. Students may confuse it with the noun alien from science fiction; show the connection (foreign, outsider) and that the verb means making someone feel like an outsider. Keep examples about school behaviors, not about real groups.
notes.va.solidarity.n: Solidarity is unity among people who share a cause. Ask for actions that show it (a joint letter, a shared silence, staying with a teammate). Contrast with simply agreeing. Keep examples positive and local.
notes.va.integrate.v: Integrate means bringing parts or groups into one whole. In social contexts it implies equality and mutual change. Distinguish from assimilate. Students may also meet integrate in math (calculus); mention it without teaching it.
notes.va.marginalize.v: Marginalize means pushing people to the edge of decisions or attention. Model marginal + -ize and point to the margin of a page. Practice with school scenarios that involve access, such as meeting times or buildings, and ask for fixes.
notes.va.persona.n: Persona is the public face someone shows, such as an online image or a stage character. Not all personas are false; they can be roles. Ask students to compare a persona with the person behind it. In Spanish, persona means person; the English word is a false friend.
notes.va.introspective.adj: Introspective means looking inward. Model intro- + spect + -ive: look inside. Connect to journal writing and to literary narrators. Do not treat introspective as shy or sad; it means thoughtful about oneself.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The word marginalize has marginal in it, and the margin is the edge of a page. If a group marginalizes someone, it pushes the person to the edge. In the passage, Mr. Bell says a small club should not be marginalized, so he asks for a page in the yearbook. That makes the club visible instead of leaving it at the edge.'
discuss: What is the difference between a community that asks you to assimilate and one that tries to integrate everyone?
How can you show solidarity with someone without speaking for them?
misconceptions: Assimilate, conform, and integrate all mean the same thing.
Alienate only refers to creatures from space.
extend: Write a journal entry from the point of view of a character who feels alienated, then rewrite it after someone shows solidarity.
Create a web of your own identity with at least five parts, and choose one part to explain in a paragraph (private details may be fictional).
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit assimilate, conform, and integrate within two days by sorting short scenarios, and at one week in a written reflection. The earlier words testimony, context, conscience, and perception return when students read a memoir or a personal account and decide how much context they need to understand it.

wida.oral: Partner A describes a short school scenario about a new student. Partner B names which word fits (assimilate, conform, integrate, alienate, marginalize, or solidarity) and explains why.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: identidad, asimilar, ascendencia (ancestry; linaje is another choice), conformarse, hacer sentir ajeno (alienate; alienar can suggest mental illness in some regions), solidaridad, integrar, marginar, personaje (persona; Spanish persona means a person, so the false-friend risk should be taught), introspectivo.
Cognate flags for identidad, asimilar, conformarse, solidaridad, integrar, marginar, and introspectivo should be confirmed.
Facts: Cedar Hills, Noor, Mr. Bell, and the chess club are fictional. The passage does not name any real culture or country.

Sense boundaries: integrate also has a math sense and conform has a legal sense, mentioned only in teacher notes or examples. Morphology: alien + -ate and marginal + -ize are shown as bases plus suffixes; no further etymology is claimed.
